transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-01-22 15:00 PST | Duration: ~72m | Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Dr. Elena Marquez (Helix), Tom Bauer (Helix), Asha Patel (Helix CTO)

[00:00] Jordan: hey everyone thanks for joining, uh we're gonna run through the quantization review for the Helix models, happy to kick off.
[00:18] Elena: thanks. we sent over the eval set and some failure cases - the clinical NER examples where we saw entity dropouts after int8 conversion.
[00:27] Priya: yeah we saw those, thanks. quick agenda: recap your workload, show AWQ and GPTQ runs we did, talk fp8 possibilities, runtime impacts on latency/throughput, and then ops questions (VPC/on-prem). sound good?
[00:40] Tom: yep that works. main constraints: latency < 120ms tail per request for our 512-token worst case, and no PHI leaves the VPC. also limited to A100 40GB nodes on prem.
[00:55] Jordan: got it. quick Q - are you using long prefix contexts a lot? I ask because KV cache behavior matters with quantized runtimes.
[01:05] Elena: yes we have long patient notes, typical context windows are 2k to 4k tokens in some flows.
[01:12] Priya: okay that's important. initial notes: AWQ-int8 gave 2.0-2.3x throughput vs fp16 on our small bench for 2k context, but we saw a 1.5-2.5 point drop on exact-match entity recall on the NER set for one of your prompts.
[01:30] Asha: can you repeat AWQ, sorry?
[01:33] Priya: AWQ - A W Q, it's the newer int8 recipe that uses asymmetric per-channel quant with row-wise scaling. compared to GPTQ which is more of a per-tensor or per-channel offline quant with weight-only/fine-tune knn calibrations. The tradeoff: AWQ tends to preserve LM output quality better on many tasks while being faster at runtime, but there's still corner-case regressions.
[01:58] Tom: are those regressions systematic? meaning same entities always drop?
[02:04] Priya: in our runs it's correlated with rare tokens and with positional-sensitive layers (some of the later attention layers). for Helix specifically the entity labels with punctuation were more affected.
[02:16] Elena: we noticed drop in recalls for hyphenated gene names and some abbreviations.
[02:22] Jordan: typical mitigations - keep embeddings and final layer in fp16, quantize most transformer weights to int8, and optionally keep softmax/norms in fp16. That hybrid approach gives a better accuracy/latency sweet spot.
[02:37] Priya: yeah we validated a hybrid config: embed + layernorm + lm_head in fp16, rest in AWQ-int8. that reduced the NER recall gap to ~0.6-1.1 points, while still ~1.8x throughput.
[02:53] Asha: how about fp8? is that a reasonable path? we have some A100s but fp8 support is patchy.
[03:00] Priya: FP8 (e4m3 / e5m2) looks promising - better fidelity than int8 in some cases and smaller memory than fp16. but hardware support is limited; on A100 you don't get native fp8, you'd emulate which kills perf. Hopper/H100 has more native support. So for your on-prem A100s, fp8 isn't practical unless you upgrade.
[03:22] Tom: so AWQ-int8 is the more pragmatic option for now?
[03:26] Jordan: yes for A100 fleets AWQ-int8 or GPTQ-int8 are common. GPTQ often requires per-layer search and can be slower to produce, but sometimes yields slightly better quality on code/long-range tasks. AWQ is faster to apply and sometimes better in commonsense tasks.
[03:44] Elena: you mentioned GPTQ sometimes is better - is that tunable per-model?
[03:49] Priya: we run both recipes on onboarding. For some models GPTQ's per-channel quant with clotting corrections helps. But GPTQ needs more calibration data and takes longer to produce the quantized artifact. AWQ tends to be more deterministic in our infra runs.
[04:05] Tom: how do these quant methods affect KV cache size and latency?
[04:10] Priya: runtime-wise, quantized weights reduce memory footprint which can reduce GPU memory pressure and decrease cold-starts for KV cache. But at inference time, INT8 math paths might need dequant + compute + requant in some kernels which adds a small per-token latency. On our lib, AWQ-int8 added ~6-12ms per token vs pure fp16 in a single-stream low-batch setting, but the throughput gains at batch >8 are large so p50 improves.
[04:39] Jordan: important nuance: continuous batching in production will amortize dequant overhead. If you have many concurrent requests, batching will push throughput up and per-token latency drops. But for Helix's tail latency requirement we need to tune batching thresholds and warm KV cache aggressively.
[04:59] Elena: is prefix/KV cache correctness affected by quantization? we saw slightly different completions when reusing cache vs fresh runs.
[05:07] Priya: correctness shouldn't change due to cache itself; differences come from small numeric shifts in attention scores after quantization which can cascade especially for long prefixes. Also beam/gen determinism across quant variants isn't perfect. We recommend re-run some of your cache-heavy flows in the quantized artifact to validate.
[05:24] Tom: ok. in the perf numbers you shared, what was the hardware and sequence length?
[05:29] Priya: A100 40GB, batch 1 to 16 tests, context 2k tokens. For batch=1 single-stream, AWQ-int8 increased per-token latency ~9ms but throughput for batch=8 was 2.1x vs fp16. We can share the raw perf sheet.
[05:45] Asha: for compliance we need to ensure that quantization artifacts can be reproduced and the process is auditable. can you outline the build pipeline?
[05:53] Jordan: yes, our standard pipeline is: export fp16 weights -> run GPTQ/AWQ offline script with calibration data (we store seed + dataset manifest) -> produce quant artifact with metadata (hashes, layer configs) -> package into container with runtime flags. We include a provenance file that lists calibration set, random seeds, sweep configs.
[06:12] Elena: do you support HSM/KMS to keep model keys and avoid exfil?
[06:16] Jordan: yes for Private deployments we integrate with customer KMS/HSM; encryption at rest and access control is supported, and we can run under customer VPC with no model artifacts leaving the network unless approved.
[06:27] Priya: ops note: if you do on-prem, we recommend bringing a small test dataset and letting us run the quant pipeline in your lab to measure the actual regressions.
[06:36] Tom: sounds good. what about automated evals for regression detection?
[06:40] Priya: Redwood Optimize can run prompt sets and compute regressive alerts. For you we'd use the clinical NER + summarization rubric, measure F1/EM and human review for edge cases. We can set alert thresholds.
[06:51] Elena: on the quality front, is there a quick way to reduce regression after quantizing if we see a drop?
[06:57] Priya: few levers: 1) hybrid fp16 for sensitive layers, 2) larger calibration set or targeted calibration for rare tokens, 3) selectively GPTQ a couple of layers instead of AWQ across the board, 4) use per-channel scaling and bias corrections.
[07:15] Asha: any risk of hallucination increase post-quant?
[07:18] Priya: small shifts in logits can change tokenization paths, so yes hallucination patterns can change. We recommend human-in-the-loop eval for high-sensitivity outputs, and adding heuristics or rerankers if needed.
[07:30] Tom: what about fp8 again - if in the future we move to H100, would fp8 be the recommended path?
[07:36] Jordan: for H100 and newer, fp8 is compelling: often similar or better fidelity than int8, with lower memory than fp16. The runtime needs to support it; Redwood runtime has experimental fp8 kernels and we can run QA.
[07:48] Elena: are there best-practice quant configs for LLaMA-style models vs decoder-only models you tested?
[07:54] Priya: generally LLaMA-style weights quantize well with AWQ; decoder-only autoregressive models need careful handling of rotary embeddings and attention scales. We keep rotary params in fp16 sometimes. Also watch out for embedding tables which are sensitive for NER.
[08:11] Tom: any effect on checkpoint size for model rollouts?
[08:15] Priya: quant artifacts are typically 2-4x smaller depending on recipe; AWQ-int8 roughly halves memory vs fp16, GPTQ sometimes compresses further depending on sparsity. That helps with faster deploys across your fleet.
[08:28] Jordan: ops question - do you want us to run a focused A/B with your golden set and live traffic?
[08:34] Elena: yes, but first we'd like a offline 1k-sample run to get baseline numbers.
[08:38] Priya: we'll do that. My plan: run AWQ-int8, GPTQ-int8, and hybrid fp16 configs on the 1k set and return perf + F1/EM breakdown by entity type.
[08:49] Asha: timeline?
[08:51] Jordan: Priya will run bench by Friday 1/29. We'll share build notes earlier (1/26). Then plan on-prem run first week of Feb.
[08:59] Tom: network question - for on-prem, do you need direct access or we provide a jump host?
[09:04] Jordan: either works; jump host is fine but we prefer an isolated lab network with KMS access for testing. We'll send a network checklist.
[09:12] Elena: also can you include notes about per-layer fallback if we see regressions in production?
[09:16] Priya: yes, we'll include how to flip specific layers back to fp16 on the runtime without re-quantizing the whole model - it's a runtime flag in our runtime that layers can be promoted to fp16 at load time.
[09:27] Jordan: cool, should we talk about some of the sample numbers we saw on your sample?
[09:30] Priya: quick callout: on one prompt with 2k context the AWQ-int8 config gave identical summary but missed two short tokens in NER; GPTQ-int8 closed the gap but increased quantization build time by ~3x. We captured diffs.
[09:46] Asha: ok is there a recommended default?
[09:48] Priya: start AWQ-int8 with hybrid fp16 for embeddings/norms, run automated evals, then if needed try GPTQ on top layers.
[09:57] Tom: any implications for batching strategy? we have bursty traffic.
[10:01] Priya: for bursty traffic we recommend low-latency tail targets: small batching thresholds + micro-burst policy to avoid long queueing. For heavy throughput windows, increase batch window to benefit int8 throughput. We can provide recommended autoscale and batch policies for Dedicated deployments.
[10:19] Jordan: quick follow-up on determinism - if you require exact reproductions, we can pin RNG seeds, but quantized numeric shifts can still cause divergent paths depending on batching and parallelism.
[10:31] Elena: got it. any security concerns with quant artifacts?
[10:35] Jordan: same as other artifacts - store in customer-controlled bucket, sign artifacts, and use KMS to encrypt. On private deployments we can avoid pushing artifacts to Redwood-managed stores.
[10:45] Priya: ok to wrap with next steps?
[10:48] Elena: yes please.
[10:49] Jordan: recap: Priya runs 1k-sample bench (AWQ, GPTQ, hybrid) by 2026-01-29; Jordan shares AWQ/GPTQ build notes and perf sheet by 2026-01-26; schedule on-prem run week of 2026-02-02; Jordan to send SOC2/KMS docs by 1/25.
[11:10] Asha: thank you, that sounds good.
[11:13] Tom: thanks all.
[11:15] Jordan: thanks everyone we'll follow up in email with artifacts and a calendar invite for the on-prem slot. bye.

[End of transcript]
